Coordinate_Note: Study area spans 33 islands in northern Solomon Islands; region centroid only.
Description: Five vegetated reef islands vanished entirely between 1947 and 2014 and six more were severely eroded. Shoreline recession destroyed two villages that had existed since at least 1935, forcing community relocations.
Source: Albert et al., Environmental Research Letters 11:054011 (2016)

Description: Home to 25 families. Has lost more than half its habitable area, with 11 houses washed into the sea since 2011.
Source: Albert et al. (2016), summarised by the authors in The Conversation

Coordinate_Note: Island point not confirmed. Coordinates are for the Kia archipelago, Isabel Province, the study area of Albert et al. (2016) where Nararo lies. Verify before publication.
Description: Village abandoned as the sea moved inland; the community rebuilt on the hilltop away from the coast.
Source: Reporting on Albert et al. (2016)

Coordinate_Note: French Frigate Shoals centroid; East Island itself lay approx. 23.78N 166.22W before 2018.
Description: An 11-acre strip of sand and gravel washed away by Hurricane Walaka's storm surge in October 2018; only two slivers of land re-emerged. Key nesting site for green sea turtles and pupping ground for endangered monk seals. Whale-Skate Islet was lost to erosion in the 1990s and Trig Island eroded earlier in 2018.
Source: NASA Earth Observatory

Coordinate_Note: Cakaudrove Province centroid; village point not confirmed. Village sits on Natewa Bay.
Description: Community of around 150 people moved 2 km uphill in 2014 after successive seawalls failed and saltwater intrusion ruined coconut, breadfruit and banana cultivation. One of the first completed planned relocations in the Pacific.
Source: Kaldor Centre Climate Mobility Hub; McMichael et al., The Geographical Journal (2019)

Description: Seven families welcomed into storm-resilient housing on higher ground in November 2020. The process took nearly a decade from first discussions in 2011.
Source: Kaldor Centre Climate Mobility Hub

Coordinate_Note: Ha'apai comprises 51 islands; group centroid.
Description: Coastal erosion has carved up to 40 metres of land off the island. In Hihifo District, reduced ENSO-linked rainfall combined with saltwater intrusion into the groundwater aquifer has left very little freshwater.
Source: Earth.Org Tonga profile; Tonga PACC Joint National Action Plan

Description: Villagers observed in 2007 that their coastline had retreated by roughly 50 metres since 1997.
Source: EBSCO Research Starters synthesis

Description: Identified as likely to become the first provincial capital globally to relocate residents and services due to sea-level rise. Local rise runs 7-10 mm/yr, roughly three times the global average.
Source: Albert et al., Environmental Research Letters 11:054011 (2016)

Coordinate_Note: Atoll spans ~70 km from Luaniua (SE) to Pelau (N).
Description: One of the world's largest atoll groups: 120 low coral islands enclosing a 70 km lagoon, with around 3,000 residents. Swamp taro, coconut and other traditional food sources under threat; relocation may be the only option. Some 600 people of Ontong Java descent already live without permanent homes at the Lord Howe Settlement in Honiara.
Source: Earth Journalism Network

Description: The most instrumented atoll flooding site in the world. The March 2014 wave event overwashed the seaward side, raising groundwater and salinizing the freshwater lens. After the December 2008 overwash the main well drew full-strength seawater within two days and water remained non-potable for a further 22 months.
Source: Storlazzi et al., Science Advances 4:eaap9741 (2018); Gingerich, Voss & Johnson, J. Hydrology (2017); USGS flood-depth dataset

Coordinate_Note: Atoll capital; Majuro atoll extends over ~100 km of reef.
Description: At 1 metre of sea-level rise, 40% of existing buildings would be endangered and 96% of the city subject to frequent flooding. High-tide flooding projected to rise from 2 to 20 events per year.
Source: World Bank & Government of RMI, Adapting to Rising Sea Levels in Marshall Islands (2021)

Location: Runit Island & Runit Dome, Enewetak Atoll
Description: A 115 m concrete dome built 1977-80 caps more than 120,000 tons of material contaminated by US nuclear testing, including plutonium. Cracks in the cap have raised concern about vulnerability to encroaching seas. Most of Runit Island sits about 2 m above sea level, with roughly 1 m of rise projected by 2100. A 2024 DOE Pacific Northwest National Laboratory investigation found storm surge and gradual rise would be the biggest factor spreading radionuclides through the atoll. DOE maintains the dome is not in imminent danger of collapse.
Source: ABC News (March 2026); DOE Report to Congress

Description: Remains too contaminated to inhabit, including Bikini Island, the Marshall Islands' highest-lying atoll. Nuclear legacy has removed the country's most elevated land from the adaptation options.
Source: ABC News (March 2026)

Coordinate_Note: Tarawa (capital atoll) used as the reference point. Kiribati spans 33 atolls across 3.5 million sq km, so a true country centroid would fall in open ocean far from any population.
Description: Sea level rose 5-11 cm over the past 30 years, with a further 15-30 cm likely by 2050 and 50-100 cm by 2100. Areas with fewer than five high-tide flood days per year today face an average of 65 annually by the 2050s.
Source: NASA Sea Level Change Team, Closer Look: Kiribati (2025)

Description: At high tide the ocean surges up through the porous ground, flooding the country's only international airport runway. Areas with fewer than five flood days per year today could average 25 by the 2050s.
Source: NASA/JPL (2024); ABC News (May 2026)

Coordinate_Note: Masig Island shown. Boigu approx. 9.25S 142.22E; Poruma 10.05S 143.07E; Warraber 10.21S 142.82E.
Description: The UN Human Rights Committee found in Billy et al. v. Australia (2022) that Australia violated Islanders' rights to culture and to freedom from arbitrary interference with private, family and home life through inadequate climate protection. On Masig, saltwater seepage has diseased coconut trees and killed the fruit. The Committee noted a 10-15 year window for affirmative measures including relocation.
Source: UN Human Rights Committee, CCPR/C/135/D/3624/2019 (23 Sept 2022)

Coordinate_Note: Atafu shown. Nukunonu approx. 9.17S 171.80W; Fakaofo approx. 9.38S 171.22W.
Description: All three atolls sit a maximum of two metres above the high-water level of ordinary tides, across 12 sq km of land with about 1,500 residents. Atafu suffered significant inundation and erosion during Cyclone Percy in 2005. Community research identified seawall construction and edge planting as priorities for staying in place.
Source: UNDRR; University of Auckland Tokelau country summary (2024)

Coordinate_Note: Lagoon surface area ~822 sq miles containing 15 main islands.
Description: Densely populated with the vast majority of people living on the immediate coastline. December 2008 tidal surges flooded homes and businesses, prompting a presidential emergency declaration and evacuations.
Source: Permanent Mission of FSM to the UN

Location: Woleai, Eauripik, Satawan, Lukunor, Kapingamarangi, Nukuoro, Utwe & Malem
Coordinate_Note: Federated States of Micronesia country centroid. Row covers eight dispersed sites spanning >1,500 km, from Woleai (approx. 7.4N 143.9E) to Kapingamarangi (approx. 1.1N 154.8E); split into separate rows if mapping individually.
Description: Adaptation Fund project providing climate-resilient infrastructure to help communities relocate from high-risk coastal inundation sites, alongside water security and flood/drought risk reduction. Kapingamarangi and Nukuoro are Polynesian outlier atolls among the country's lowest-lying land.
Source: Adaptation Fund, Enhancing the Climate Resilience of Vulnerable Island Communities in FSM

Coordinate_Note: Pago Pago harbour; Faga'itua Bay lies approx. 10 km east.
Description: Post-2009 earthquake land subsidence is estimated to produce roughly twice as much sea-level rise by 2060 as climate change alone, putting coastal impacts decades ahead of comparable Pacific communities. Modelling predicts rising seas will escalate nearshore extreme water levels as the fringing reef loses capacity to dissipate wave energy. High-tide flooding projected to rise from 0 to 102 events per year.
Source: Pacific Islands CASC; Barnes et al., Scientific Reports (2024)

Description: High-tide flooding projected to increase from 5 to 43 events per year.
Source: WMO, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific

Description: High-tide flooding projected to increase from 5 to 34 events per year.
Source: WMO, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific

Coordinate_Note: Territory centroid.
Description: High-tide flooding projected to increase from 2 to 22 events per year.
Source: WMO, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific

Coordinate_Note: Avatoru village approx. 14.94S 147.70W.
Description: High-tide water levels modelled under SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 across twelve islands show lagoon-side land loss on several. On Avatoru, urbanisation, swamp and coastal reclamation and sediment extraction destabilised the lagoon coast, while intense beach mining drove rapid ocean-side shoreline retreat.
Source: Duvat, Magnan et al., Scientific Reports 12 (2022)

Description: Of 931 houses surveyed across Rangiroa and Tikehau, more than 61% sit in areas that experienced at least one substantial marine inundation event since the 1980s. Based on 106 interviews.
Source: Magnan, Ranche, Duvat et al., VertigO (open access, French)

Coordinate_Note: Vunisavisavi shown (near Savusavu, Vanua Levu). Muani is a separate village; coordinates not confirmed.
Description: At Vunisavisavi, shoreline erosion threatens homes and a sacred gravesite, with residents planting mangroves as coastal defence. At Muani, the seawall is now overtopped, culverts filled and imported rock and sand eroded away; the village has decided to move.
Source: Washington Post field reporting (August 2025)

Coordinate_Note: Fiji country centroid, on Viti Levu. Row covers 800+ at-risk communities across the archipelago, not a single site.
Description: Over 800 communities identified as at climate risk, with 48 villages requiring partial or full relocation. An August 2025 reassessment raised the eventual figure to as many as 676 communities, with 17 villages on a red list for urgent intervention. Legal mandate set by the Climate Change Act 2021, working with the CROC Trust Fund (2019) and the 2018 Planned Relocation Guidelines.
Source: Fiji Planned Relocation Guidelines (2018); Standard Operating Procedures for Planned Relocation (2023)

Coordinate_Note: Abaiang atoll centroid; Tebunginako village lies on the atoll's western side.
Description: Abandoned in 1994; residents relocated about 50 m inland and the original site now sits roughly 30 m offshore. Taro pits more than 200 m from the coast are being killed by king tides. CAVEAT: a South Pacific Applied Geoscience Commission technical report (Webb, 2006) attributed the primary cause to natural erosion from an ocean/lagoon channel blocked by villagers over a century earlier.
Source: Government of Kiribati climate portal; Webb, SOPAC technical report (2006)

Location: Lateu / Lataw village, Tegua Island (Torres Islands)
Coordinate_Note: Tegua island point; relocated settlement (Lirak) sits approx. 600 m inland.
Description: Village moved several hundred metres inland in 2002-04 with Vanuatu government and Canadian aid; a 2005 UNEP release described the residents as perhaps the world's first climate change refugees. CAVEAT: a PNAS study found that from 1997 to 2009 absolute sea level rose 150 +/- 20 mm while the islands themselves subsided 117 +/- 30 mm, tectonic motion nearly doubling the apparent rise.
Source: Ballu et al., PNAS (2011); UNEP release via UN News

Location: Carteret Islands (Han, Huene, Piul, Iolasa, Iangain)
Description: Peak elevation just 1.5 m. Tulele Peisa, formed by the Council of Elders in 2006, is organising voluntary relocation of around 3,300 people to Tinputz, Tearouki and Mabiri on Bougainville. K14 million sought to move 350 families, with no government funding contributed as of 2022. CAVEAT: erosion, tectonic subsidence and population pressure all contribute.
Source: UNU Our World; PINA; Boege & Rakova (2023)

Coordinate_Note: Takuu (Mortlock) Atoll shown as the central of the three. Nuguria approx. 3.3333S 154.7500E; Tasman (Nukumanu) approx. 4.5311S 159.4294E. Split into separate rows if mapping individually.
Description: Roughly 2,500 people facing the same combination of pressures as the Carteret Islands.
Source: Boege & Rakova, Challenges and Pitfalls of Resettlement

Coordinate_Note: Reclaimed platform runs 780 m along the lagoon shoreline.
Description: The flagship Pacific land-building project. From December 2022, sand dredged from the lagoon built a platform 780 m long and 100 m wide (about 7.8 ha), designed to stay above sea-level rise and storm waves beyond 2100. A second phase completed a further 8 hectares of reclaimed, elevated land in October 2025, funded at US$17.5m by Australia, New Zealand and the United States. TCAP 1B is planned for the northern shoreline.
Source: UNDP Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project; Green Climate Fund FP015

Coordinate_Note: Nanumaga shown. Nanumea approx. 5.6614S 176.1036E.
Description: Berm Top Barriers, geotextile bags filled with sand raising the natural storm berm by an extra 1.5 m, built along 665 m and 1,330 m of foreshore respectively to protect homes, schools, hospitals, farmland and cultural assets.
Source: UNDP Pacific

Coordinate_Note: Eastern end of South Tarawa; project site not independently confirmed.
Description: The most ambitious plan attempted, and a cautionary tale. Designed to reclaim 300 hectares of swampy land and raise it 2-5 m to house 35,000 people, resilient to projected 2200 ocean levels. New Zealand's MFAT dropped funding in 2021 as costs escalated; roughly NZ$4.2m of a NZ$20m budget had been spent and the project stalled.
Source: Jacobs project page; Stimson CORVI Tarawa assessment

Coordinate_Note: South Tarawa spans roughly 30 km of atoll rim.
Description: Covers water supply management, mangrove replanting, protection of public infrastructure, strengthened laws to reduce coastal erosion and settlement planning. Two desalination plants began construction in April 2022 with ADB, World Bank, GCF and GEF support.
Source: Stimson CORVI Tarawa assessment; SPC Kiribati adaptation briefing

Coordinate_Note: Langa Langa Lagoon shown. Lau Lagoon approx. 8.4636S 160.8528E on the northeast coast.
Description: Centuries-old artificial islands built by hand from coral and stone, now facing the sea that once protected them. About 12,000 people live across the two lagoons; Langa Langa contains thirteen islands along a 21 km lagoon and Lau Lagoon around 60. On Busu Island (pop. 300) high tides now flood most of the island almost every month. Residents on Raolo are building their island higher and planting mangroves; Busu's community weighs the cost of buying and shipping stone from the mainland.
Source: ReliefWeb / IPS; EMKP Fera i asi documentation project

Description: Typhoon Ophelia cut total island land area by about 5%, yet between 1976 and 2006, 73 of 87 islands increased in size, and by 2010 total landmass exceeded the pre-typhoon area by nearly 4%. NOTE: area gain does not raise island elevation.
Source: Ford & Kench (2016), Anthropocene

Coordinate_Note: Marshall Islands country centroid. Row covers six atolls and two mid-ocean reef islands across the RMI.
Description: Since the mid-20th century, 39.74% of shoreline accreted versus 17.23% eroded, with islands growing from 9.09 sq km to 9.46 sq km between WWII and 2010. Accretion has slowed from 0.77 m/decade to 0.29 m/decade. The authors stress adaptation plans need this dynamism understood to avoid maladaptation.
Source: Ford & Kench, Multi-decadal shoreline changes in response to sea level rise in the Marshall Islands, Anthropocene (2015)

Coordinate_Note: Also known as Knox Atoll, southeast of Mili Atoll in the southern RMI.
Description: Ford & Kench (2014) tracked island recovery following a 1905 typhoon and found an entirely new island had formed, with others still recovering over a century later.
Source: Ford & Kench (2014), cited in Ford & Kench (2015)

Coordinate_Note: Tuvalu country centroid. Row covers all 101 islands across nine atolls, not a single site.
Description: A 2.9% net increase in land area (73.5 ha) over four decades, with 74% of islands increasing in size and land area increasing on eight of nine atolls, despite local sea level rising at twice the global average. NOTE: area gain does not raise island elevation.
Source: Kench, Ford & Owen, Nature Communications (2018)

Coordinate_Note: Pacific and Indian Ocean atolls.
Description: Duvat's 2019 review of 709 islands across 30 atolls found 73.1% stable in area, 15.5% increased and 11.4% decreased. In FSM, analysis of 104 islands across 16 atolls found 46% of shorelines with statistically significant accretion.
Source: Duvat (2019), WIREs Climate Change; Sengupta, Ford & Kench (2021), Geomorphology
